question: How can one slow movement laugh and cry at the same time?
intro: The Fourth’s slow movement alternates a serene G-major theme with a lamenting second theme, varying each in turn. Its coda erupts in E major, opening the door to the finale, before subsiding to a quiet G-major close. Listen for how much the quiet passages hold and how suddenly the tempo can change.

sections.label: A′ · Anmuthig bewegt
sections.mNote: theme returns livelier, over pizzicato basses

sections.label: B′ · Klagend returns
sections.mNote: lament returns in cor anglais, parts set against each other

sections.label: A″ · Final variation
sections.mNote: theme now with sudden changes of tempo and metre

cues.title: Cellos sing the theme
cues.text: The cellos, in two groups, sing a long, serene theme in G major over plucked basses and sustained violas. It is marked “sehr gesangvoll” — very singing — and begins at a whisper.
cues.evidence: Full score (IMSLP70999), PDF p. 78 (printed p. 304): cellos “pp espress., sehr gesangvoll”, violas sustained (bowed), double basses pizzicato. Report: the file opens at −41 dB, rises to −30 dB by 0:05, and attack density stays at or below 0.6 per second through the first minute, with G and D major estimates.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A motionless, meditative line
cues.text: Follow the plucked bass beneath the theme. The Mahler Foundation hears a passacaglia bass under this motionless, meditative melody: the same slow steps return while the line above them keeps unfolding.
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation’s movement page describes the opening theme as “motionless and meditative with its passacaglia bass”: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-4/symphony-no-4-movement-3-ruhevoll-poco-adagio/ . Full score, PDF p. 78: double basses pizzicato. Report: at 0:35–0:45 the level is restrained (−30.4 to −29.4 dB) and attacks are sparse (0.0–0.4 per second). The passacaglia reading comes from the source and score, not from the report, which cannot identify instruments.

cues.title: A smile on a tomb
cues.text: In 1901 Mahler described this Adagio: St Ursula presides with a smile, like that on the stone effigies of knights and prelates in churches, hands joined. Its character, he said, is “solemn, blessed peace; serious, gentle gaiety”.
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation’s introduction quotes Mahler’s 1901 description of the Adagio: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-4/symphony-no-4-introduction/ . Basinger gives Bruno Walter’s title “Saint Ursula Laughs As Well”: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/

cues.title: His mother’s face
cues.text: While writing this movement Mahler sometimes saw his own mother’s face “smiling through her tears” — a woman who, he felt, had been able to solve and forgive all suffering by love.
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation’s introduction reports this recollection of the composition: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-4/symphony-no-4-introduction/

cues.title: Oboe joins; violins take the tune
cues.text: At rehearsal 1 an oboe adds a soft counter-line marked “zart”, and the violins take over the cellos’ tune. The sound brightens as the theme rises into a higher register.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 78: rehearsal 1, first oboe “zart, p espress.”, violins entering. Basinger describes a violin countermelody moving to the oboe so that the violins can take the cello tune: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/ . Report: brightness rises from 1.4 kHz at 1:30 to 2.46 kHz at 1:40 and level from −26.6 dB at 1:30 to −19.8 dB at 1:45.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The texture thins
cues.text: After the violins’ phrase the texture thins to soft sustained notes. The level drops by about nine decibels at 1:50 and attacks all but stop; the music hangs on held harmonies.
cues.evidence: Report: relative level falls from −19.8 dB at 1:45 to −29.0 dB at 1:50 and attack density is 0.0–0.4 per second through 2:15.

cues.title: Sketched in days at Aussee
cues.text: Mahler drafted the first three movements in about ten days at the end of his 1899 holiday at Bad Aussee, after cold, wet weather and a rented villa within earshot of a bandstand. He put the sketches in a drawer until the next summer.
cues.evidence: Basinger says the first three movements were drafted in about ten days at the end of the 1899 break: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/ . The Mahler Foundation describes the cold, wet weather, the villa near the bandstand and the sketches left in a desk drawer until the following summer: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-4/symphony-no-4-introduction/

cues.title: High violins over soft harmony
cues.text: From about 2:50 the violins hover high above the harmony, with bassoons and horns supporting below. The brightness rises above 2.4 kHz while the level stays very quiet.
cues.evidence: Report: spectral brightness is 2463–2789 Hz from 2:50 to 3:10 at −32.2 to −25.7 dB, compared with about 1.5 kHz at 2:20–2:40. Full score, PDF p. 79: first violins written high, marked ppp–pp, with bassoons and horns. The page is placed by proportion.

cues.title: A swell and a glow
cues.text: A brief swell lifts the theme to its warmest point around 3:15, and again between 3:30 and 3:40. Notice how little the tempo moves while the sound grows.
cues.evidence: Report: relative level is −20.9 dB at 3:15 and −21.0 to −19.3 dB at 3:30–3:40, against −26.3 and −26.9 dB at 3:20–3:25; key estimates read G major (r 0.96) at 3:20 and C major at 3:35.

cues.title: Links to the finale
cues.text: Mahler rebuked a critic who ignored the symphony’s thematic ties: each of the first three movements, he wrote, is “joined thematically with the last one in a most intimate and meaningful way”. The Adagio’s coda announces the finale’s main motif.
cues.evidence: Basinger quotes Mahler’s letter to Georg Göhler about the thematic connections: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/ . The Mahler Foundation says the coda announces the principal motif of the final movement: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-4/symphony-no-4-movement-3-ruhevoll-poco-adagio/

cues.title: A hush before the lament
cues.text: The theme dwindles to near silence, with almost no attacks, and the harmony leans towards the minor. The second theme is about to break the calm.
cues.evidence: Report: relative level is −31.9 to −25.6 dB and attack density is 0.2–0.4 per second from 4:00 to 4:25; key estimates move to B minor at 4:25.

cues.title: The lament: klagend
cues.text: At rehearsal 2 the tempo drops to “Viel langsamer” — much slower — and an oboe sings “klagend, sehr ausdrucksvoll”: lamenting, very expressive. The second theme has descending, chromatic lines and sighing figures.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 80 (printed p. 306): rehearsal 2, “Viel langsamer”, oboe “klagend, sehr ausdrucksvoll”. Basinger describes the second theme’s descending lines, chromatic inflections and sigh figures: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/ . Report: key estimates read B minor at 4:25–4:35 and brightness falls under 1 kHz at 4:30–4:35; boundary at 4:46 (novelty 0.61).
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The violins sing the lament
cues.text: The violins take the lament “singend” — singing — with the instruction “nicht schleppen”, do not drag. Attacks rise to nearly two a second as the accompaniment moves, and the key estimates settle on E minor.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 80, second system: “singend”, “Nicht schleppen”. Report: attack density 1.2, 1.8 and 1.2 per second at 4:45–4:55; E minor estimates r 0.85–0.92.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Flowing over plucked strings
cues.text: At “Fliessend” — flowing — plucked cellos and basses keep a quiet pulse while the woodwinds play above. Mahler adds “etwas drängend”, somewhat pressing, as the line gathers strength.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 81 (printed p. 307): “Fliessend”, pizzicato cellos and basses, oboe and clarinet lines, then “Etwas drängend”. Report: brightness rises from about 1.6 kHz at 5:25 to 2.1 kHz at 5:30 as the pace of the music increases.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The first outburst
cues.text: Marked “Etwas drängend. Leidenschaftlich”, the music surges. Flutes, oboes, clarinets and bassoons rise to fortissimo over a climbing bass, and the lament reaches its first peak.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 81, second system: rehearsal 3, “a tempo”, “Etwas drängend. Leidenschaftlich”, ff in the woodwinds with a rising bass and a bass clarinet change. Report: relative level climbs from −26 dB at 5:30 to −19.2 dB at 5:35 and −15.9 dB at 5:40.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Horns and trumpets, bells up
cues.text: A second wave brings horns and trumpets, marked “Schalltrichter auf” — bells up — for a fortissimo outburst. The level peaks near 6:40, the loudest point so far.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 82 (printed p. 308): horns and trumpets “Schalltrichter auf”, ff, with timpani. Report: relative level rises from −16.2 dB at 6:10 to −9.2 dB at 6:40, the highest level up to that point.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Dying away
cues.text: The outburst subsides at once: the level falls by about fifteen decibels in ten seconds, from −14.7 dB at 6:50 to −29.6 dB at 7:00. Mahler marks “Etwas zurückhaltend” and then “Wieder langsam”.
cues.evidence: Report: relative level is −14.7 dB at 6:50, −19.6 dB at 6:55 and −29.6 dB at 7:00, a fall of 14.9 dB. Full score, PDF p. 82: “Etwas zurückhaltend”, “Rit.”, “Wieder langsam”.

cues.title: The theme returns: Anmuthig bewegt
cues.text: “Anmuthig bewegt” — gracefully moving — brings back the first theme in livelier dress. Plucked cellos and basses keep a gentle step beneath clarinets and violas, and attacks jump from none to about two a second.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 83 (printed p. 309): “Anmuthig bewegt”, pizzicato divided cellos and basses, clarinets and violas “espress.”. Report: attack density 0.0 at 6:55–7:00, then 1.4 at 7:05 and 2.0 at 7:15.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Slightly more animated, never a dance
cues.text: Mahler asks that the variation begin very moderately and grow somewhat livelier as it goes. Listen for the pulse quickening only a little: this is grace, not a dance.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 83: “Anmuthig bewegt” with the note that it is at first very moderate and in the course of the variation gradually somewhat livelier. Report: attack density 0.6–2.0 per second across 7:05–7:45.

cues.title: St Ursula laughs too
cues.text: Bruno Walter titled this movement “Saint Ursula Laughs As Well”, a line from the finale’s poem: the most serious of the saints, he wrote, only smiles. Mahler himself voiced the same associations.
cues.evidence: Basinger quotes Walter’s letter of 5 December 1901 and notes that the associations of Freund Hein and St Ursula were voiced by Walter and elsewhere by Mahler: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/

cues.title: A swell inside the variation
cues.text: Near 8:45 the variation swells to about −15 dB, its own high point, before the music quietens again. The warmth is a matter of sound, not speed.
cues.evidence: Report: relative level is −23.3 dB at 8:35, −18.2 dB at 8:40, −15.3 dB at 8:45 and −19.8 dB at 8:50; key estimates read D major (r 0.85–0.90) at 8:35 and 8:45–8:50.

cues.title: A short peak, then a darkening
cues.text: A brief peak near 9:20 interrupts the calm. Afterwards the music thins and darkens: by 9:40 the level is about −29 dB and the key estimates lean towards E♭ and G minor.
cues.evidence: Report: relative level is −16.7 dB at 9:15, −13.9 dB at 9:20 and −21.5 dB at 9:25, then −29.1 dB at 9:40; key estimates read E♭ major at 9:45 and G minor from 9:55.

cues.title: The lament returns
cues.text: At rehearsal 6, “Langsam”, the lament comes back in a darker colour. The cor anglais and oboe sing it, marked “klagend”, and the key estimates swing to G minor. Mahler sets pieces of the theme against each other, so it sounds more fragmented.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 88 (printed p. 314): rehearsal 6, “Langsam”, English horn and oboe “klagend”. Basinger describes the variation setting portions of the theme against one another: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/ . Report: a strong boundary at 9:42 (novelty 0.98); G minor estimates from 9:55.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The climb begins
cues.text: From about 10:15 the music starts to climb. Attacks multiply, and after a brief dip by 10:25 the level has risen by about seven decibels at 10:35 as the lament pushes upward.
cues.evidence: Report: relative level is −22.0 dB at 10:15, −26.7 dB at 10:25 (a separate trough) and −14.7 dB at 10:35, a rise of 7.3 dB from 10:15; attack density rises from 0.4 to 1.0 per second between 10:05 and 10:20.

cues.title: A long climactic plateau
cues.text: The lament reaches a fortissimo plateau that lasts for about half a minute. The score drives the strings to fff while the winds answer with bells raised; this is the tragic climax Basinger describes.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 89 (printed p. 315): rehearsal 7 with ff and fff in the strings, bells-up woodwind writing, horns and timpani; Basinger describes the variation still leading to the tragic climax. Report: relative level is −9.2 dB at 10:50 and −9.0 dB at 10:55, staying near −13 to −9 dB until 11:20.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Keys drift widely
cues.text: Through the climax the harmony wanders: the estimates pass through C♯ minor and A♭ minor. The Mahler Foundation calls this section unstable in tonality, chromatic and modulating through many keys.
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation page says the second lament section has a rather unstable tonality, moving through many keys: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-4/symphony-no-4-movement-3-ruhevoll-poco-adagio/ . Report: key estimates read C♯ minor at 11:00–11:10 and A♭ minor at 11:15–11:20.

cues.title: The last peak
cues.text: A final peak near 11:55, about −8 dB, is the loudest moment of the lament and one of the five loudest windows in the file. A long descent follows.
cues.evidence: Report: 11:55 is one of the five loudest five-second windows (−8.0 dB), with −10.4 dB at 11:50 and −14.2 dB at 12:00.

cues.title: Sinking into silence
cues.text: The lament dissolves. From 12:10 the level falls by about seventeen decibels in half a minute, to about −35 dB at 12:40. Mahler marks it “molto dim.”, and the instruments die out one by one.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 92 (printed p. 318): “molto dim.”, “morendo”, “zurückhaltend” and pppp. Report: relative level is −18.4 dB at 12:10 and −35.0 dB at 12:40, a fall of 16.6 dB.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The final variation: Andante
cues.text: At rehearsal 9 the last statement of the theme begins “Andante”: the cellos sing it, bowed, over plucked violas and basses, while the clarinets rest. Mahler is about to change the tempo and metre without a word of warning.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 93 (printed p. 319): rehearsal 9, “Andante”, bowed cello melody, pizzicato violas and double basses, and eight opening bars of rest in the clarinet staff. Report: boundary at 12:46 (novelty 0.63) with D and G major estimates r 0.71–0.74.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Without the slightest transition
cues.text: The score says “ohne die geringste Vermittlung” — without the slightest mediation — and the music jumps to “Allegretto subito”. In this last variation Basinger hears the metre change as well as the pace. Attacks leap from almost none to about two a second.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 93: “Allegretto subito (Nicht eilen). Ohne die geringste Vermittlung plötzlich das neue Tempo.” Basinger describes the switch from duple time into a three-beat pattern, with three graduated increases of tempo: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/ . Report: attack density 0.2 at 13:25, 1.4 at 13:30 and 2.0 at 13:35.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Tempo changes in steps
cues.text: Further changes arrive “as suddenly and surprisingly as before”, as a note in the score puts it. The music speeds up in steps; the density of attacks peaks near 13:50 at about three and a half a second.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 94 (printed p. 320): “Der Tempowechsel vollzieht sich ebenso plötzlich und überraschend wie vorhin.” Report: attack density is 2.2 at 13:45, 3.6 at 13:50 and 3.0 at 13:55.

cues.title: Allegro molto
cues.text: At “Allegro molto (subito)” the music is at its fastest. Piccolo and glockenspiel sparkle above racing violins, and the level climbs to about −9 dB near 14:25, among the loudest passages so far.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 96 (printed p. 322): “Allegro molto (subito). Wieder mit plötzlichem Übergange”, piccolo, glockenspiel and spiccato strings. Report: relative level is −23.5 dB at 14:05, −14.1 dB at 14:10 and −8.8 dB at 14:25.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Andante subito
cues.text: “Andante subito. Ganz plötzlich das Anfangstempo der Variation” — quite suddenly, the variation’s opening tempo — drops the music from its peak to near silence. The level falls by about fifteen decibels in fifteen seconds.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 96, right edge: “Andante subito. Ganz plötzlich das Anfangstempo der Variation”. Report: relative level is −9.3 dB at 14:30 and −24.0 dB at 14:45; boundary at 14:32 (novelty 0.56).

cues.title: The slow tempo restored
cues.text: For the next two minutes the pace is the slow opening one again: “Poco adagio”, then “Wieder a tempo (Ruhig)”. The music is hushed, divided strings sing “zart”, and long notes stretch across the bar lines.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 97 (printed p. 323): “Poco adagio”, “Zart”, “Wieder a tempo (Ruhig)”, strings divided in three or two. Report: relative level spans −36.0 to −20.3 dB and attack density is 0.0–0.2 per second from 14:50 to 16:45, with G major estimates.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Cheerfulness with something eerie
cues.text: In October 1901 Mahler told Natalie Bauer-Lechner that the symphony holds “the cheerfulness of a higher and, for us, unfamiliar world that holds something eerie and horrifying”. The finale’s child, he said, explains how everything is meant.
cues.evidence: Basinger quotes Mahler’s remark to Bauer-Lechner in October 1901: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/

cues.title: A breath before the blaze
cues.text: Listen for the silence ahead. The strings are “zart”, tender; then “Vorwärts. Poco più mosso” — forwards, a little faster — leads to “Luftpause”, a breathing pause, before the coda.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF pp. 97–98 (printed pp. 323–324): “Zart”, “Vorwärts. Poco più mosso” and “Luftpause!” at rehearsal 12. Report: level −33.6 to −30.6 dB at 16:15–16:45 before the jump at 16:50.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: E major breaks in
cues.text: After the “Luftpause” the key jumps to E major at fortissimo. Strings roll and sweep, marked “viel Bogen”, with the harp gliding beneath. The Mahler Foundation calls it the symphony’s only genuinely loud tutti.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 98 (printed p. 324): rehearsal 12, “Vorwärts. Poco più mosso”, four-sharp signature, “viel Bogen”, harp glissandi. Report: level jumps from −23.1 dB at 16:50 to −6.9 dB at 16:55 (strongest boundary, novelty 1.00, 16:54); E major estimates r 0.77–0.94 at 16:55–17:30. The Mahler Foundation quote is on its movement page: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-4/symphony-no-4-movement-3-ruhevoll-poco-adagio/

cues.title: Bells up: the finale’s motif
cues.text: Horns and trumpets, marked “Pesante” with their bells raised, sound a broad theme over pounding timpani. It recalls the first movement’s development tune and announces the finale’s main motif.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 100 (printed p. 326): “Pesante”, “Schalltrichter auf”, timpani with two mallets. Basinger identifies the horn melody as recalling the first movement’s development theme and anticipating the finale; the Mahler Foundation says the coda announces the finale’s principal motif. Report: level spans −12.6 to −7.8 dB at 17:00–17:30.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Gone in a breath
cues.text: At 17:35 the glare vanishes: the level falls by about nine decibels and the sound is hushed again. The blaze has lasted only about forty seconds.
cues.evidence: Report: relative level is −12.6 dB at 17:30, −21.6 dB at 17:35 and −25.4 dB at 17:40; the E major jump was at 16:54–16:55.

cues.title: Booed in Munich
cues.text: Mahler conducted the first performance in the Kaim-Saal, Munich, on 25 November 1901, with the soprano Margarethe Michalek. The audience, expecting another monumental symphony, found the Fourth’s innocence baffling, and the performance was roundly booed.
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation’s concert record names the venue, orchestra and soloist: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/locations/germany/munich/1901-concert-munich-25-11-1901/ . Its introduction describes the audience’s reaction: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-4/symphony-no-4-introduction/

cues.title: Harmonics high above
cues.text: From about 18:50 the brightness rises to about 2.2–2.8 kHz at a very low level. The violins are playing harmonics, “Flag.”, in four divisions, marked “Allmählich wieder zurückhaltend” — gradually holding back again.
cues.evidence: Report: spectral brightness is 2172–2772 Hz at 18:50–19:10 at −37.4 to −31.2 dB, with G major estimates. Full score, PDF p. 101 (printed p. 327): violins in four divisions with “Flag.”, “Allmählich wieder zurückhaltend”.

cues.title: Dying away completely
cues.text: The last direction is “gänzlich ersterbend” — dying away completely. The movement closes quietly in G major, and the recording’s level falls steadily through the last seconds.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 101: “Gänzlich ersterbend”, “morendo”, closing in G major. Report: relative level is −40.5 dB at 19:55 and −60.4 dB at 20:00, falling further afterwards; local key estimates at 19:30–19:55 read G major, E minor and D major and are not used for the harmony.

transitions.title: Much slower, and the oboe laments
transitions.how: The first theme thins out and is marked “Zurückhaltend” — holding back — as muted strings and soft winds sustain. At rehearsal 2 Mahler writes “Viel langsamer”, and an oboe enters “klagend, sehr ausdrucksvoll” in a descending, chromatic line; the clarinets exchange their B♭ instruments for ones in A. The key turns to the minor, and the tune’s sighing figures replace the first theme’s long, level phrases. Tempo and mode change together, with almost nothing bridging them.
transitions.evidence: Full score (IMSLP70999), PDF pp. 79–80 (printed pp. 305–306): “Zurückhaltend”, rehearsal 2, “Viel langsamer”, oboe “klagend, sehr ausdrucksvoll”, clarinets “in A”, muted lower strings. Report: level −31.9 to −25.6 dB at 4:00–4:25, key estimates B minor at 4:25–4:35, boundary at 4:46 (novelty 0.61).

transitions.title: Brass fall silent; the theme dances
transitions.how: The lament’s second climax, with horns and trumpets bells up, breaks off into “Etwas zurückhaltend”, a ritardando and “Wieder langsam”, and the music is marked “Immer noch zurückhaltender” — still more held back — down to pp. Then comes “Anmuthig bewegt”, the first theme in quicker notes: pizzicato divided cellos and basses step beneath clarinets and violas. The join works by a collapse in volume followed by a change from sustained to moving lines.
transitions.evidence: Full score, PDF pp. 82–83 (printed pp. 308–309): “Etwas zurückhaltend”, “Rit.”, “Wieder langsam”, “Immer noch zurückhaltender”, “Anmuthig bewegt”. Report: level −14.7 dB at 6:50 to −29.6 dB at 7:00, attack density 0.0 to 1.4 per second at 7:05.

transitions.title: Cor anglais takes up the lament
transitions.how: The variation slows and fades: “zurückhaltend”, with the violins on the G string and the lower strings “morendo”, and the key signature changes. At rehearsal 6 the marking is “Langsam” with the beat unchanged, and the cor anglais — joined by an oboe — plays the lament “klagend” over quiet strings, with horns adding soft harmony. A new instrumental colour and a darker key do the work of a bridge, and the lament’s parts are set against each other rather than sung straight.
transitions.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 88 (printed p. 314): “zurückhaltend”, “G-Saite”, “morendo”, rehearsal 6 “Langsam”, English horn and oboe “klagend”. Report: a strong boundary at 9:42 (novelty 0.98) with levels −30.5 to −22.0 dB at 9:45–10:15 and E♭ / G minor estimates in that span.

transitions.title: The lament dies; Andante begins
transitions.how: After the climax the lament collapses: “molto dim.”, timpani and clarinets “morendo”, strings to pppp. At rehearsal 9 the first theme returns marked “Andante”: the cellos carry it, bowed, over plucked violas and basses, and the clarinets, silent at first, join later. Mahler will then jump, “ohne die geringste Vermittlung”, to Allegretto in three-beat metre, then to Allegro molto and back, always without a transition. The join into this variation is a quiet restart; the shocks follow once the theme is established.
transitions.evidence: Full score, PDF pp. 92–93 (printed pp. 318–319): “molto dim.”, “morendo”, pppp, rehearsal 9 “Andante”, “Allegretto subito”, “Ohne die geringste Vermittlung plötzlich das neue Tempo”. Report: level falls to −35.0 dB at 12:40; boundary at 12:46 (novelty 0.63); attack density jumps at 13:30.

transitions.title: A breath, then E major at fortissimo
transitions.how: The strings, muted and at ppp, fall away into a “Luftpause” — a breath-pause — and rehearsal 12 is marked “Vorwärts. Poco più mosso”. The key jumps to E major, four sharps, at fortissimo: violins, violas and cellos roll in repeated figures marked “viel Bogen” while the harp glides beneath, and bells-up horns and trumpets follow. No harmonic bridge is needed because the pause itself isolates the new key; the shock comes from loudness, register and orchestral weight all changing at once.
transitions.evidence: Full score, PDF pp. 97–98 (printed pp. 323–324): “Zart”, “Dämpfer ab”, “Luftpause!”, “Vorwärts. Poco più mosso”, four sharps, “viel Bogen”, harp glissandi. Report: level −33.6 to −30.6 dB at 16:15–16:45, then −23.1 dB at 16:50 and −6.9 dB at 16:55; strongest boundary at 16:54 (novelty 1.00).

source.locator: PDF pp. 78–101 (printed pp. 304–327), rehearsal figures 1–13; changes are placed at the recording’s existing passage anchors and are approximate.

timeline.note: Cellos, in two groups, sing the theme over sustained violas and plucked basses; the violins and winds are silent.
An oboe adds a soft counter-line as the violins take the cellos’ tune.
Divided violins float high; bassoons and horns support, with the harp touching in a few notes.
An oboe sings the lament with bassoon and horn support; the clarinets change to instruments in A. Before this the strings had faded muted; their mutes come off.
The violins take up the lament “singend”, with the lower strings and winds moving beneath.
Woodwinds rise to fortissimo above trembling strings and a climbing bass.
Horns and trumpets with bells raised drive the lament to its first brass climax; timpani roll beneath.
Clarinets and violas carry the livelier theme over plucked cellos and basses.
Cor anglais and oboe voice the lament; horns and low strings add soft harmony.
Full strings, wind chords and horns drive the lament to its peak; timpani roll.
Clarinets, horns and soft timpani dwindle with the strings to pppp.
A bowed cello melody begins the final variation over plucked violas and basses; the clarinets rest and join later.
Violins and violas spin light figures in the sudden three-beat Allegretto.
Racing violins, piccolo and glockenspiel mark the Allegro molto.
Divided strings sing the slow theme “zart” with soft horns and clarinets beneath.
E major breaks in: rolling strings, harp glissandi and a full wind and timpani tutti.
Horns and trumpets sound the broad “Pesante” melody with bells raised.
Harp and divided strings return to a whisper, “sehr zart und innig”.
Violins in four parts play harmonics high above soft winds and harp.

composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee, and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony anticipates Mahler’s so closely that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony. The cantata Das klagende Lied, written at eighteen and nineteen, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881, and Mahler turned to the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
